## Question 1 (2 points)

Compute the joint probability that someone is a current smoker and they have Type 2 diabetes. Also compute the joint probability that someone is a non-smoker and they have Type 2 diabetes.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
diabetes_data <- read.csv("../Datasets/diabetes_data.csv")
attach(diabetes_data)
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mean(Smoking_Status == "Current smoker" & Diabetes_Type == "Type 2")

mean(Smoking_Status == "Non-smoker" & Diabetes_Type == "Type 2")
```

## Question 2 (2 points)

Compute the conditional probability that someone has Type 2 diabetes given that they exercise regularly. Also compute the probability that someone has Type 2 diabetes given that they do not exercise at all.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mean(Diabetes_Type[Exercise_Frequency == "Regularly"] == "Type 2")

mean(Diabetes_Type[Exercise_Frequency == "None"] == "Type 2")
```

## Question 3 (4 points)

We are interested in three probabilities: 1) The probability someone is a current smoker, 2) the probability that someone exercises occasionally, and 3) the probability that someone is a current smoker and exercises occasionally. Compute these probabilities below using the diabetes dataset.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mean(Smoking_Status == "Current smoker")

mean(Exercise_Frequency == "Occasionally")

mean(Smoking_Status == "Current smoker" & Exercise_Frequency == "Occasionally")
```

Using the definition of independence and based solely on these numbers, would we say that exercising occasionally is independent of being a current smoker?

[The definition of independence says that the product of the marginal probabilities should equal the joint probability. In this case we have $0.35 \times 0.24 = 0.084 \neq 0.11$ suggesting that these are not independent.]{style="color: red;"}

## Question 4 (4 points)

We are interested in three probabilities: 1) The probability someone has Type 2 diabetes, 2) the probability that someone's fasting blood sugar is above 100, and 3) the probability that someone has Type 2 diabetes and their fasting blood sugar is above 100. Compute these probabilities below using the diabetes dataset.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mean(Diabetes_Type == "Type 2")

mean(Fasting_Blood_Sugar > 100)

mean(Diabetes_Type == "Type 2" & Fasting_Blood_Sugar > 100)
```

Using the definition of independence and based solely on these numbers, would we say that having Type 2 diabetes and having a fasting blood sugar above 100 are independent?

[The definition of independence says that the product of the marginal probabilities should equal the joint probability. In this case, we have $0.28 \times 0.21 = 0.0588 \neq 0.08$ so these would not be independent.]{style="color: red;"}
